items.stem: In IGCSE First Language English compositions, how are the marks divided?
options: Content and structure, and Style and accuracy
items.answer: Content and structure, and Style and accuracy
items.markingKey: Compositions are marked for Content and structure (W1–W2) and Style and accuracy (W3–W5).

items.stem: Explain why this extract would score poorly on W2 (organise and structure ideas and opinions for deliberate effect): ‘First I will talk about the cost. Also uniforms are smart. Another thing is cost again. In conclusion uniforms.’
items.answer: Ideas are poorly organised: points repeat, there is no logical sequence and the conclusion is undeveloped.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the specific weakness; links it to W2; suggests how it could be improved.

items.stem: Explain why this extract would score poorly on W2 (organise and structure ideas and opinions for deliberate effect): ‘Then this happened and then that happened and then we went home and then it was the end.’
items.answer: The narrative has no shaping: events are listed with ‘and then’, with no development, pace or deliberate effect.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: identifies the specific weakness; links it to W2; suggests how it could be improved.

items.stem: Improve this extract so that it meets W3 (use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures appropriate to context) more successfully, then explain one change you made: ‘The market was busy. There were lots of people. It was noisy. There were lots of stalls.’
items.answer: Model: Shoppers jostled between the stalls, haggling over mangoes and bolts of indigo cloth, while a radio blared from somewhere behind a mountain of melons. The weakness was that vocabulary is vague (‘lots of’) and every sentence is a short simple sentence, so there is no range of vocabulary or sentence structure.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: a rewrite that clearly addresses W3; meaning kept or developed; explanation of the improvement; no new errors.

items.stem: Improve this extract so that it meets W5 (make accurate use of spelling, punctuation and grammar) more successfully, then explain one change you made: ‘Despite the rain. We carried on walking, we was soaked by the time we reached the hut.’
items.answer: Model: Despite the rain, we carried on walking; we were soaked by the time we reached the hut. The weakness was that a sentence fragment, a comma splice and an agreement error (we was).
items.markingKey: Award up to 5 marks from: a rewrite that clearly addresses W5; meaning kept or developed; explanation of the improvement; no new errors.

items.stem: ‘Young people today have too much choice.’ Write an argument for or against this view. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: clear stance; developed reasons with evidence; counter-argument rebutted; cohesive paragraphs; strong conclusion.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): a clear, sustained point of view; well-developed reasons supported by evidence; counter-arguments anticipated and rebutted; logical, cohesive paragraphs and a strong conclusion; middle band (2): a clear view with some supporting reasons and evidence; some development; paragraphs mostly logical; lower band (1): a simple view with few or undeveloped reasons; limited organisation. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: clear stance; developed reasons with evidence; counter-argument rebutted; cohesive paragraphs; strong conclusion.

items.stem: What is a periodic sentence?
options: A sentence that uses a full stop
A sentence in which the main clause is delayed until the end
A sentence with no subordinate clause
items.answer: A sentence in which the main clause is delayed until the end
items.markingKey: It builds suspense or emphasis by holding back the main point.

items.stem: This is a compound-complex sentence: ‘Although the evidence was strong, the jury hesitated, and the court waited.’ Explain its effect.
items.answer: Compound-complex sentence: the structure holds tension across several clauses.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying compound-complex sentence; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: the structure holds tension across several clauses.

items.stem: This is a complex sentence: ‘When the lights flickered, the room fell silent.’ Explain its effect.
items.answer: Complex sentence: the subordinate clause sets up the condition for the main event.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for identifying complex sentence; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: the subordinate clause sets up the condition for the main event.

items.stem: Identify the sentence structure in ‘The door opened.’, explain its effect, and write a sentence of your own about a storm using the same structure.
items.answer: Simple sentence: a single main clause gives a stark, sudden effect. Own sentence: any accurate simple sentence about a storm.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for simple sentence; 1 for effect; remaining mark(s) for an accurate original example.

items.stem: Identify the sentence structure in ‘She ran.’, explain its effect, and write a sentence of your own about a storm using the same structure.
items.answer: Simple sentence: the brevity mirrors the sudden action. Own sentence: any accurate simple sentence about a storm.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for simple sentence; 1 for effect; remaining mark(s) for an accurate original example.

items.stem: Write a descriptive piece about a train pulling out of a station, using a deliberate variety of sentence structures (including at least one periodic sentence and one minor sentence) to control pace and atmosphere. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: open with a long, cumulative sentence that establishes a train pulling out of a station; shift to short sentences at the key moment; end with a minor sentence or a periodic sentence for impact.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): a vivid, coherent picture built through carefully selected sensory detail and imagery; strong atmosphere; deliberate shifts of focus give structure; middle band (2): a clear description with some effective detail and imagery; some atmosphere; may drift into narrative; lower band (1): a list-like description with limited detail and little atmosphere; may turn into a story. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: sentence structures varied purposefully; pace controlled; atmosphere sustained; no slide into narrative.

items.stem: What does it mean to say vocabulary is ‘precise’?
options: The same word is repeated for clarity
Each word is chosen to convey exactly the intended meaning or effect
The longest possible words are used
items.answer: Each word is chosen to convey exactly the intended meaning or effect
items.markingKey: Precision beats length: ‘limped’ is more precise than ‘walked slowly’.

items.stem: Replace ‘said’ in ‘He said he was not guilty.’ with ‘muttered’. What does the new word suggest?
items.answer: ‘muttered’ is more precise: speech verbs reveal attitude and tone.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: valid connotation of the new word.

items.stem: In ‘The food smelled good.’, compare the effect of replacing ‘good’ with ‘sweet’ and with ‘pungent’.
items.answer: Both are more precise than ‘good’; precise adjectives create a specific sensory impression.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: connotation of ‘sweet’; connotation of ‘pungent’; comparison of the impressions created.

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence so that its register suits a speech to a school assembly, and explain two choices you made: ‘Data indicates a statistically significant correlation between sleep duration and academic attainment.’
items.answer: Model: Here is something worth knowing: the more you sleep, the better you are likely to do in your exams.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: register appropriate to a speech to a school assembly; meaning kept; two explained choices (vocabulary, contractions, sentence length, address).

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence so that its register suits a blog post for young travellers, and explain two choices you made: ‘Visitors are advised to exercise caution when utilising public transport after dark.’
items.answer: Model: Heads up: take care on buses and trains late at night – stick to busy carriages and keep your bag close.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: register appropriate to a blog post for young travellers; meaning kept; two explained choices (vocabulary, contractions, sentence length, address).

items.stem: Write two short texts on the same subject: (1) a letter of complaint to a sports shop; (2) a review of the same shop for a website read by teenagers. Then write a paragraph analysing how and why your vocabulary and register differ. Write about 250–350 words in total.
items.answer: Model approach: text 1 formal (full forms, polite modals, precise nouns, clear purpose and sign-off); text 2 informal and lively (direct address, contractions, colloquial but controlled language); analysis naming specific choices and linking them to audience and purpose.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): both texts precisely judged for audience and purpose; analysis perceptive and specific; middle band (3–4): two recognisably different registers; analysis identifies some choices; lower band (1–2): register barely changes; analysis vague. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (2): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: formality markers; vocabulary choice; sentence length; modes of address; purpose.

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The results, were clear the experiment had failed.
The results were: clear the experiment had failed.
The results were clear: the experiment had failed.
The results were clear, the experiment had failed.
items.answer: The results were clear: the experiment had failed.
items.markingKey: A colon after a complete clause introduces the explanation.

items.stem: Identify and explain the error in this sentence, then correct it: ‘Neither of the candidates have answered the question.’
items.answer: Error: agreement: ‘neither’ takes a singular verb. Corrected: ‘Neither of the candidates has answered the question.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: names the error; explains the rule; gives a correct version.

items.stem: Identify and explain the error in this sentence, then correct it: ‘I would of come if I had known.’
items.answer: Error: ‘would of’ should be ‘would have’. Corrected: ‘I would have come if I had known.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: names the error; explains the rule; gives a correct version.

items.stem: Proofread this paragraph and rewrite it with all errors corrected: ‘As the train pulled into the station their was a sudden silence. Nobody moved, everyone was watching the man on the platform. He was holding a sign, it said only one word: Welcome. Who was he waiting for.’
items.answer: Model: ‘As the train pulled into the station, there was a sudden silence. Nobody moved; everyone was watching the man on the platform. He was holding a sign that said only one word: Welcome. Who was he waiting for?’
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: comma after fronted clause; their → there; comma splice → semicolon; comma splice → relative clause; question mark. Deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Proofread this paragraph and rewrite it with all errors corrected: ‘Me and my sister was walking home when we seen the fire. We run to the nearest house, and phoned the fire brigade who arrived in minutes.’
items.answer: Model: ‘My sister and I were walking home when we saw the fire. We ran to the nearest house and phoned the fire brigade, who arrived in minutes.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: Me and my sister → My sister and I; was → were; seen → saw; run → ran; comma placement before relative clause. Deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Answer the following questions on accuracy (W5). (a) Write two sentences of your own about a journey: one using a semicolon correctly and one using a colon correctly. (b) Explain why accurate punctuation matters for the reader, with one example of how a comma can change meaning.
items.answer: (a) Any two accurate sentences, e.g. ‘The road was flooded; we turned back.’ / ‘We had one hope left: the night bus.’ (b) Punctuation controls meaning and clarity, e.g. ‘Let’s eat, Grandma’ versus ‘Let’s eat Grandma’.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark reason; 1 mark example [2]

items.stem: What is cohesion in writing?
options: The way sentences and paragraphs are linked so that the text flows logically
items.answer: The way sentences and paragraphs are linked so that the text flows logically
items.markingKey: Created by connectives, reference words, repetition and topic sentences.

items.stem: Explain how cohesion is achieved in: ‘The council announced a new recycling scheme. This initiative will begin in June.’
items.answer: ‘This initiative’ refers back to ‘a new recycling scheme’, linking the sentences without repetition.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the cohesive device; explains how it links ideas.

items.stem: Explain how cohesion is achieved in: ‘Many students struggle with sleep. Such problems often affect concentration.’
items.answer: ‘Such problems’ summarises the previous idea and links it to its consequences.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: identifies the cohesive device; explains how it links ideas.

items.stem: These paragraph topics for a descriptive composition about a harbour from dawn to night are jumbled. A: dawn: stillness and first light B: evening: return of the boats C: midday: heat and emptiness D: night: lights on water, quiet E: morning: boats leaving and noise building Put them in the most effective order and explain the structural principle you used.
items.answer: AECBD – chronological shifts in time.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: correct or justifiable order (AECBD); explanation of the structural principle (chronological shifts in time); comment on the effect of the opening and ending.

items.stem: These paragraph topics for a discursive essay on school uniforms are jumbled. A: introduction: the debate B: evaluation: compromise options C: arguments against: cost and self-expression D: conclusion: reasoned judgement E: arguments for: equality and identity Put them in the most effective order and explain the structural principle you used.
items.answer: AECBD – balanced structure leading to evaluation.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: correct or justifiable order (AECBD); explanation of the structural principle (balanced structure leading to evaluation); comment on the effect of the opening and ending.

items.stem: Composition task: Write a discursive essay on whether cities or villages offer a better life. Write a paragraph plan (one line per paragraph), then write the composition. Use topic sentences and a range of cohesive devices, and make at least one deliberate structural choice. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: a 4–6 paragraph plan; paragraphs linked by discourse markers and reference chains; a deliberate structural choice (e.g. one-line paragraph, circular ending, delayed revelation).
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): both sides explored fairly and in depth with evidence; points weighed against each other; a reasoned judgement reached in the conclusion; cohesive paragraphing; middle band (2): both sides covered with some development; structure clear though weighing of points is limited; lower band (1): mainly one side or a list of points; little development or evaluation. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: plan followed; paragraphing logical and purposeful; cohesive devices varied; structural choice deliberate.

items.stem: Which objective is mainly assessed by the overall shape and paragraphing of a piece?
items.answer: W2
items.markingKey: W2: organise and structure ideas and opinions for deliberate effect.

items.stem: Explain why this extract would score poorly on W1 (articulate experience and express what is thought, felt and imagined): ‘The sunset was nice and I felt good.’
items.answer: The writer does not convey the experience, thoughts or feelings in a developed, imaginative way; ‘nice’ and ‘good’ say almost nothing.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: identifies the specific weakness; links it to W1; suggests how it could be improved.

items.stem: Improve this extract so that it meets W2 (organise and structure ideas and opinions for deliberate effect) more successfully, then explain one change you made: ‘First I will talk about the cost. Also uniforms are smart. Another thing is cost again. In conclusion uniforms.’
items.answer: Model: begin with the strongest point (cost), develop it with evidence, then move to a second distinct point (identity), and end with a conclusion that weighs them. The weakness was that ideas are poorly organised: points repeat, there is no logical sequence and the conclusion is undeveloped.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: a rewrite that clearly addresses W2; meaning kept or developed; explanation of the improvement; no new errors.

items.stem: Which sentence structure is used here? ‘Heat, dust, flies, silence.’
items.answer: minor sentence
items.markingKey: Minor sentence: a verbless list builds a harsh atmosphere quickly.

items.stem: Explain how the writer varies sentence structure for effect in: ‘The corridor stretched ahead, lined with doors that had not been opened for years, each one stamped with a faded number, each handle dull with dust. I reached for number nine. Locked.’
items.answer: A long, cumulative sentence slows the pace and builds atmosphere; the short sentence and the one-word minor sentence ‘Locked.’ halt the reader abruptly, creating frustration and suspense.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: identifies the structures; effect on pace/tension/emphasis; credit for linking structure to meaning.

items.stem: Rewrite this passage, varying the sentence structures to create a more powerful effect. ‘She found the letter. She read it. She cried.’
items.answer: Model: When she finally found the letter – tucked inside the cover of her father’s old atlas – she read it standing up, too afraid to sit. Then she cried.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: Award for a deliberate range of structures (e.g. fronted clauses, periodic sentence, minor sentence) that clearly enhances effect; accurate punctuation. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Replace ‘good’ in ‘The food smelled good.’ with ‘fragrant’. What does the new word suggest?
items.answer: ‘fragrant’ is more precise: precise adjectives create a specific sensory impression.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: valid connotation of the new word.

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence so that its register suits a formal letter to a newspaper editor, and explain two choices you made: ‘Honestly, the new car park is a total joke and it’s wrecking the town centre.’
items.answer: Model: I believe the new car park is seriously damaging the character and economy of the town centre.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: register appropriate to a formal letter to a newspaper editor; meaning kept; two explained choices (vocabulary, contractions, sentence length, address).

items.stem: Write two short texts on the same subject: (1) a report to the council on litter in a park; (2) a leaflet for children encouraging them to use the bins. Then write a paragraph analysing how and why your vocabulary and register differ. Write about 250–350 words in total.
items.answer: Model approach: text 1 formal (full forms, polite modals, precise nouns, clear purpose and sign-off); text 2 informal and lively (direct address, contractions, colloquial but controlled language); analysis naming specific choices and linking them to audience and purpose.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): both texts precisely judged for audience and purpose; analysis perceptive and specific; middle band (3–4): two recognisably different registers; analysis identifies some choices; lower band (1–2): register barely changes; analysis vague. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (2): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: formality markers; vocabulary choice; sentence length; modes of address; purpose.

items.stem: Identify and explain the error in this sentence, then correct it: ‘Each team must bring their own equipment, and they must arrive on time, they will be disqualified otherwise.’
items.answer: Error: comma splice and pronoun consistency. Corrected: ‘Each team must bring its own equipment and arrive on time; otherwise, it will be disqualified.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: names the error; explains the rule; gives a correct version.

items.stem: Proofread this paragraph and rewrite it with all errors corrected: ‘The documentary, which was filmed in the Amazon, show how deforestation effects local communities. It argues that goverments must act now.’
items.answer: Model: ‘The documentary, which was filmed in the Amazon, shows how deforestation affects local communities. It argues that governments must act now.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: show → shows (agreement); effects → affects; goverments → governments. Deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Answer the following questions on accuracy (W5). (a) Explain the rule broken in ‘The students books were left in the hall.’. (b) Write two sentences of your own about a journey: one using a semicolon correctly and one using a colon correctly.
items.answer: (a) plural possessive apostrophe (b) Any two accurate sentences, e.g. ‘The road was flooded; we turned back.’ / ‘We had one hope left: the night bus.’
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark rule; 1 mark correction [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain how cohesion is achieved in: ‘Engineers proposed a bridge; residents preferred a tunnel. The latter would cost twice as much.’
items.answer: ‘The latter’ refers precisely to the tunnel, avoiding repetition.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the cohesive device; explains how it links ideas.

items.stem: These paragraph topics for an argumentative essay on banning cars from city centres are jumbled. A: conclusion and call to action B: strongest reason: air quality, with evidence C: counter-argument (businesses) and rebuttal D: second reason: safety and space E: introduction and stance Put them in the most effective order and explain the structural principle you used.
items.answer: EBDCA – logical argument with rebuttal before the conclusion.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: correct or justifiable order (EBDCA); explanation of the structural principle (logical argument with rebuttal before the conclusion); comment on the effect of the opening and ending.

items.stem: Composition task: Describe the moment you arrive somewhere for the first time. Write a paragraph plan (one line per paragraph), then write the composition. Use topic sentences and a range of cohesive devices, and make at least one deliberate structural choice. Write about 350–450 words.
items.answer: Model approach: a 4–6 paragraph plan; paragraphs linked by discourse markers and reference chains; a deliberate structural choice (e.g. one-line paragraph, circular ending, delayed revelation).
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12: Content and structure 5 marks, Style and accuracy 7 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (4–5): a vivid, coherent picture built through carefully selected sensory detail and imagery; strong atmosphere; deliberate shifts of focus give structure; middle band (2–3): a clear description with some effective detail and imagery; some atmosphere; may drift into narrative; lower band (1): a list-like description with limited detail and little atmosphere; may turn into a story. Style and accuracy – top band (5–7): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: plan followed; paragraphing logical and purposeful; cohesive devices varied; structural choice deliberate.

items.stem: A student uses slang in a formal report. Which objective is most affected?
items.answer: W4
items.markingKey: W4: register appropriate to context.

items.stem: Explain why this extract would score poorly on W4 (use register appropriate to context): ‘Dear Sir, hey, I think your plan for the park is well bad and you should totally scrap it.’
items.answer: The register is far too informal for a formal letter to an official (hey, well bad, totally).
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: identifies the specific weakness; links it to W4; suggests how it could be improved.

items.stem: Improve this extract so that it meets W4 (use register appropriate to context) more successfully, then explain one change you made: ‘In my speech to the governors I will be like, guys, we really need a new library.’
items.answer: Model: Members of the board, I would like to make the case today for investing in a new library. The weakness was that the register (be like, guys) does not suit a formal speech to school governors.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: a rewrite that clearly addresses W4; meaning kept or developed; explanation of the improvement; no new errors.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What does a compound-complex sentence contain? (b) What is a periodic sentence?
items.answer: (a) at least two main clauses and at least one subordinate clause (b) A sentence in which the main clause is delayed until the end
items.markingKey: (a) E.g. ‘When it rained, we stayed in, but they went out.’ (b) It builds suspense or emphasis by holding back the main point.

items.stem: Explain how the writer varies sentence structure for effect in: ‘We waited. We waited through the morning and through the heat of the afternoon, and still the bus did not come.’
items.answer: The short opening sentence is then repeated and expanded into a longer one, mimicking the stretching time and growing frustration.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: identifies the structures; effect on pace/tension/emphasis; credit for linking structure to meaning.

items.stem: Rewrite this passage, varying the sentence structures to create a more powerful effect. ‘I went into the exam hall. I sat down. I looked at the paper. I did not know the first answer.’
items.answer: Model: Thirty rows of silent desks waited in the exam hall. I sat, turned the paper over with damp fingers and read the first question – once, twice, three times. Nothing.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: Award for a deliberate range of structures (e.g. fronted clauses, periodic sentence, minor sentence) that clearly enhances effect; accurate punctuation. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Replace ‘loud’ in ‘The noise was loud.’ with ‘shrill’. What does the new word suggest?
items.answer: ‘shrill’ is more precise: each adjective suggests a different kind of sound.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: valid connotation of the new word.

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence so that its register suits an article for a teenage magazine, and explain two choices you made: ‘It is recommended that adolescents engage in a minimum of sixty minutes of physical activity daily.’
items.answer: Model: Aim for at least an hour of moving about every day – dance, football, a long walk, whatever you enjoy.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: register appropriate to an article for a teenage magazine; meaning kept; two explained choices (vocabulary, contractions, sentence length, address).

items.stem: Write two short texts on the same subject: (1) a speech to parents about a fundraising event; (2) a social-media post for students about the same event. Then write a paragraph analysing how and why your vocabulary and register differ. Write about 250–350 words in total.
items.answer: Model approach: text 1 formal (full forms, polite modals, precise nouns, clear purpose and sign-off); text 2 informal and lively (direct address, contractions, colloquial but controlled language); analysis naming specific choices and linking them to audience and purpose.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): both texts precisely judged for audience and purpose; analysis perceptive and specific; middle band (3–4): two recognisably different registers; analysis identifies some choices; lower band (1–2): register barely changes; analysis vague. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (2): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: formality markers; vocabulary choice; sentence length; modes of address; purpose.

items.stem: Identify and explain the error in this sentence, then correct it: ‘The students books were left in the hall.’
items.answer: Error: plural possessive apostrophe. Corrected: ‘The students’ books were left in the hall.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: names the error; explains the rule; gives a correct version.

items.stem: Proofread this paragraph and rewrite it with all errors corrected: ‘Its often said that the citys oldest market is it’s heart. Every morning, hundreds of traders arrive, they set up there stalls before dawn.’
items.answer: Model: ‘It’s often said that the city’s oldest market is its heart. Every morning, hundreds of traders arrive; they set up their stalls before dawn.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Its → It’s; citys → city’s; it’s → its; comma splice; there → their. Deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Answer the following questions on accuracy (W5). (a) Correct ‘She was sat on the wall when the bus past.’ and explain why your version is correct. (b) Write two sentences of your own about a journey: one using a semicolon correctly and one using a colon correctly.
items.answer: (a) ‘She was sitting on the wall when the bus passed.’ – non-standard ‘was sat’; homophone past/passed (b) Any two accurate sentences, e.g. ‘The road was flooded; we turned back.’ / ‘We had one hope left: the night bus.’
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correction; 1 mark explanation [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain how cohesion is achieved in: ‘The first argument concerns cost. The second, and perhaps more important, concerns safety.’
items.answer: Ordinal signposts and ellipsis (‘The second [argument]’) guide the reader through the structure.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the cohesive device; explains how it links ideas.

items.stem: These paragraph topics for an argumentative essay on banning cars from city centres are jumbled. A: conclusion and call to action B: strongest reason: air quality, with evidence C: second reason: safety and space D: counter-argument (businesses) and rebuttal E: introduction and stance Put them in the most effective order and explain the structural principle you used.
items.answer: EBCDA – logical argument with rebuttal before the conclusion.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: correct or justifiable order (EBCDA); explanation of the structural principle (logical argument with rebuttal before the conclusion); comment on the effect of the opening and ending.

items.stem: Composition task: ‘Young people today have too much choice.’ Write an argument for or against this view. Write a paragraph plan (one line per paragraph), then write the composition. Use topic sentences and a range of cohesive devices, and make at least one deliberate structural choice. Write about 350–450 words.
items.answer: Model approach: a 4–6 paragraph plan; paragraphs linked by discourse markers and reference chains; a deliberate structural choice (e.g. one-line paragraph, circular ending, delayed revelation).
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12: Content and structure 5 marks, Style and accuracy 7 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (4–5): a clear, sustained point of view; well-developed reasons supported by evidence; counter-arguments anticipated and rebutted; logical, cohesive paragraphs and a strong conclusion; middle band (2–3): a clear view with some supporting reasons and evidence; some development; paragraphs mostly logical; lower band (1): a simple view with few or undeveloped reasons; limited organisation. Style and accuracy – top band (5–7): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: plan followed; paragraphing logical and purposeful; cohesive devices varied; structural choice deliberate.
